source.title: Can We Predict Alignment Before Models Finish Thinking? Towards Monitoring Misaligned Reasoning Models
source.authors: Yik Siu Chan; Zheng-Xin Yong; Stephen H. Bach

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the original refusal-direction work but does not use or test its difference-in-means direction or causal intervention. It studies predictive monitoring of refusal outcomes in reasoning models instead.
record.gate_note: The study trains logistic-regression probes on residual-stream activations to predict response safety. These results concern prediction, not whether a single difference-in-means direction mediates refusal. It does not ablate or add a direction, make a weight edit, assess jailbreak suppression of that direction, or test causal transfer. The quoted monitor prompt and harmful examples are not instructions to an AI reviewer.
record.test_reason: The study trains PCA+logistic-regression probes on final-layer residual activations to predict whether reasoning models' responses are safe or unsafe. It cites Arditi et al. only in related work and as future work on causal mediation. No difference-in-means direction is extracted, and no ablation, addition, weight edit or transfer test is run. All rows report the study's own monitoring method against baselines, not whether a refusal direction mediates refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Linear probes on CoT activations beat text monitors at predicting response safety, even from early CoT, and CoT text is often unfaithful (performative CoTs). The authors state the causal mechanism is unclear and may be correlational, and leave testing causal mediation of refusal to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses PCA-reduced residual-stream activations and trained logistic-regression probes to predict response labels. It does not use the original difference-in-means direction or its ablation/addition procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe performance varies with model, dataset, thinking budget, and amount of CoT observed. The authors report weaker results for s1.1-14B, attributing this partly to its low proportion of safe responses; XSTest also lowers s1.1-7B compliance and probe accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear probe on final-layer CoT activations predicts response safety well above the rare-class baseline across s1.1 (7B/14B/32B), R1-Qwen-7B and R1-Llama-8B, and three benchmarks. It is weaker on s1.1-14B, which has few safe examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, CoT activations linearly encode a predictive (not shown causal) signal of whether the final response will refuse.

fits_no_version.finding: A probe trained on StrongReject harmful prompts transfers to benign AlpacaEval/XSTest prompts with high accuracy, tracking the models' near-100% compliance. The exception is s1.1-7B on XSTest (85.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-based refusal predictors generalize to benign prompts without many false refusal flags.

record.problems: The authors state that the predictive relationship may be correlational rather than causal and that the mechanism remains unclear. Response labels come from LLM judges. Results concern a limited set of reasoning models fine-tuned on mathematical reasoning and one alignment behavior, refusal of harmful requests.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Early-foresight and performative-CoT analyses are not included because they measure predictive monitoring performance rather than any version of the specified direction claim.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction; no ablation or addition; no capability check.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing a direction; no adversarial training.
No separation of harmfulness and refusal representations.
No cross-language or base/instruct transfer of a direction.
No controlled variation of refusal training.
Reasoning models are studied, but only with predictive probes. The authors leave causal mediation (Arditi et al.) to future work.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. appears only as a citation; no version is tested. The main row-level error is the R1-Llama HarmBench PR-AUC baseline, which was taken from the ModernBERT row.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is identified or causally ablated/added; general capability after intervention is not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is evaluated.
No attack is tested for suppressing the refusal direction and no training against its ablation is performed.
No comparison of a single direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of the specified direction across languages, base/instruct stages, or model variants is tested.
No controlled comparison of refusal-training procedures or timing is performed.
The study evaluates reasoning models, but its predictive probes do not test whether the original single direction causally mediates refusal in those models.

rows.note: Table 1 reports this PR-AUC baseline as 76.6 ± 7.2; the probe value is 83.8 ± 6.6.
rows.check: Wrong baseline. 76.6 ± 7.2 is ModernBERT's PR-AUC. The rare-class baseline for R1-Llama-8B HarmBench is 48.9 ± 4.3, so the probe's 83.8 ± 6.6 is a clear gain, not partial.
